claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements increases local lattice distortion in equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Greater lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
Atomic-size-induced lattice misfit impedes edge dislocations more strongly than screw dislocations.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion constitutes enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
Greater dislocation resistance raises yield or flow strength.
Greater atomic size mismatch raises hardness.
At fixed phase, grain size, and processing history, hardness and yield strength will increase monotonically with atomic size mismatch.
An alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch has lower lattice distortion than otherwise comparable alloys with greater mismatch.
An alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch has lower resistance to dislocation motion, lower strength, and lower hardness.
Changing elemental selections while retaining equiatomic ratios can vary atomic size mismatch without introducing other composition-dependent strengthening variables.
Holding processing, phase, and grain size constant ensures that mechanical-property changes are due solely to atomic size mismatch.
The proposed relationship applies to both single-phase BCC and single-phase FCC equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Short-range ordering can alter strength even if it does not fundamentally change the active plastic mechanisms.
Secondary phases and grain-boundary oxides can interfere with the proposed dislocation-based relationship.
A transition from screw-dislocation-controlled to edge-dislocation-controlled strengthening may occur above a lattice-misfit threshold.
The quantitative threshold for edge-dislocation-dominated strengthening is not well established.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening and high-resolution TEM can provide a quantitative assessment of the relevant local lattice distortion.
Failure of increased mismatch to produce both measurable lattice distortion and a statistically significant strength or hardness increase would falsify the proposed causal chain.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes elemental composition to change atomic size mismatch, but the conditions and experiment assert that atomic size mismatch is the only varying factor and that resulting property changes are solely attributable to it. Changing elemental identities also changes chemistry, electronic structure, elastic properties, and potentially dislocation energetics; the cited TiZrNbHfTa evidence explicitly identifies electronic-structure and shear-modulus effects.
